answer:
**No—don’t quit now. Take the promotion and keep building on the side.**

Your 1,400 sign-ups show that you can attract interest. They don’t yet establish that couples keep using the app, pay for it, or recommend it. Three successful posts could conceal weak retention. Nine months of living expenses also buys less than nine months of experimentation once business costs and a job-search reserve are included.

The promotion has a real cost: you’re committing a year during which the app could outgrow your available time. Given the evidence provided, I’d accept that cost rather than spend your savings before establishing durable demand.

Before October 31:

- Examine July and August users: how many households still budget or reconcile expenses each month? Measure couples completing the core task, including partner participation, rather than individual logins.
- Interview ten active couples and five who stopped. Identify what they replaced, why they return, and why others left.
- If you aren’t charging, offer a paid plan and measure actual purchases.
- Confirm the promotion’s workload, the exact one-year commitment, and the bank’s outside-business and intellectual-property terms.

Assuming the bank permits the app and you can protect a sustainable weekly schedule, spend the year improving retention, testing acquisition beyond viral posts, and saving more. Find a trusted founder peer; lacking a cofounder alone shouldn’t decide this.

I’d reverse my recommendation if your existing data already shows sustained household retention, paying customers, repeatable growth, and specific opportunities that require full-time attention—and you can fund a defined experiment while preserving an emergency reserve. Those facts would justify declining the promotion and quitting. Sign-ups alone don’t.
